title: Career outline from San Angelo to Pollack and Whiteman
summary: Playing movie theaters with his mother, father's death in 1918, San Angelo, San Antonio, Peck Kelley in Houston, New York in 1927 with Red Nichols, Pollack, then Whiteman 1933-39.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Okay, whenever you're ready. Well, how did you learn trombone and develop your style? That's what I really like to know.

Well, I'll tell you, when I was, uh, pretty young, my mother and I used to play in, uh, the old silent movie theaters. We used to play for the comedies and, uh, I don't know, just trombone and piano. You know, learn more technique because I had the whole, swing the whole thing, melody and all. You know. And, uh, my mother played very good ragtime piano, which was very good for those years. Then, uh, I lost my father in 1918 with the flu. And then I went, we went to Oklahoma City. And I went one more year of, uh, school. And I went down to, uh, San Angelo to stay with my uncle. Because, uh, my mother was having a pretty rough time with us four kids, uh, making ends meet. So I went to San Angelo and worked in a theater as an operator and, uh, worked in his hillbilly band. And I went to San Angelo and, uh, I don't know, I was, I guess, uh, uh, sort of a repetition was, uh, by the word of mouth, I guess, got around. That there was, you had over in San Angelo and maybe had a little Tylenol trombone. So I got an offer to go to San Antonio. So in 1920, I went to San Antonio. And I worked in a place called Horn Palace with Terry Shan on piano and myself and banjo and drums. And, uh, I don't remember the other two. I worked there for a while and then there was a big flood. Uh, just almost, uh, wrecked San Antonio in 1921. So I went over and joined Peg Kelly in Houston. And, uh, and Peg, uh, was in those days about 40 years ahead on his piano playing. He just played wonderful. And, uh, everything I know I learned, I think, from Peg Kelly. So I stayed in Houston with him a while. And, uh, when things would get, uh, kind of, uh, quiet around Houston, sometimes I'd go up and work with Dr. Ross around Wichita Falls. And, uh, and I, he wanted to go to New York to see a friend of his, Willard Robinson. I knew him very well, too. And, uh, so we went to New York in 1927. And, uh, I've stayed up there ever since. I was very fortunate. And, uh, the very first thing meeting a dear old friend of mine, William and Norman. And, uh, he introduced me to Red Nickels and Miff Moll and, uh, Joe Van Ute and all of them. And then through, uh, them, they, we had a jam session and they liked my work. And, uh, and then on I did, you know, Red Nickels, uh, Five Penny records. And Miff Moll did the first ones. And then I came on and did the rest. And then I went with, uh, Benny Pollock. Which at that time had a wonderful band for a big band. It was, uh, uh, a band that could play big arrangements, fine arrangements, but turn around and, uh, play anything. There was a little kid with us, uh, the name of Benny Goodman. In those days he was about 18 years old. Jimmy McPartland and, uh, Bud Freeman. Ray Baduke, who's a New Orleans boy here, was, we got him on drums so Benny could, uh, uh, stand in front with a baton. And we went to the Park Central Hotel. We stayed there about a year. And, uh, and then when the 1929 crash, uh, the, the hotel discontinued music. And, uh, I stayed with Pollock until 1933. In the meantime, Benny Goodman had dropped out. Matty Metlock had taken his place. Bud Freeman had left. And, uh, Eddie Miller had taken his place. He was a band in the United States. And, uh, Hilton Lamar, I call it Nappy Lamar now. He was with us on the guitar. And, uh, that's the way it was up until about 1933 when I left. And I went with Paul Whiteman. Uh, so the, the band, uh, pulled away from Pollock. Uh, Pollock wanted to go to the West Coast and, uh, open a restaurant anyway. And they got Bob Crosby in the front of the band. And I stayed in Whiteman about, uh, from 33 to 39, six years. And I got a big band. I had, uh, 16 pieces. One time I had 18. And, uh, that was about the time that Harry James started and, uh, Gene Krupa. And, uh, so that, that was some of the finest years of swinging right along in there.
